source_text: Per rerum naturam fieri non posse, ut illud homines probentur tradere, quo caruisse creduntur Per rerum naturam fieri non posse, ut quo ipse caruit, tradat proli parens
pass_a_gloss: Through rerum nature to-become not to-be-able, so-that/as that human-beings probentur tradere, whither caruisse they-believe through rerum nature to-become not to-be-able, so-that/as whither himself caruit, tradat proli parens.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: By the nature of things, people cannot be shown to hand on what they are believed to have lost.
Augustine reports that Julian argued at length for the wild olive’s goodness as God’s creation.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded. This row is Augustine's report; Pass A glosses only the Julian words recoverable here.
